pages.x: By 1453 the eastern Roman Empire, which we call Byzantine, was little more than its capital, Constantinople, with perhaps 50,000 people left inside walls that had stood for a thousand years. All around it lay the lands of the Ottoman Turks.

Mehmed II became sultan at 19 and made Constantinople his first goal. He built a fortress on the Bosporus to cut the city off from the Black Sea, and in April 1453 surrounded it with perhaps 80,000 men.
A Hungarian engineer, Orban, had offered to make cannon for the Byzantines, who could not pay. Mehmed could. Orban cast a bronze giant over 8 metres long that fired stone balls of half a tonne.
pages.fx: It could fire only a few times a day, but the guns pounded the old walls day after day for six weeks.

pages.x: Inside, the emperor Constantine XI had about 7,000 defenders, among them 700 soldiers from Genoa under Giovanni Giustiniani. A great iron chain across the Golden Horn kept the Ottoman fleet out of the harbour.

Mehmed found a way round the chain. On 22 April his men hauled some 70 ships overland on greased logs, over the hill from the Bosporus into the Golden Horn. The defenders woke to see an enemy fleet inside their harbour.

Before dawn on 29 May the Ottomans attacked in waves. When Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried away, the defence broke and the janissaries poured in. Constantine XI threw off his imperial robes and died fighting. His body was never surely found.

Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia, for 900 years the greatest church in Christendom, and had it made a mosque. He made Constantinople his capital and brought in people from all over his empire to fill it again.

The fall ended the Roman Empire nearly 1,500 years after Augustus and made the Ottomans a great power for centuries. Greek scholars fled to Italy with ancient books, feeding the Renaissance, and the city became Istanbul.
pts: The end of the Roman Empire
